info.name: Orebit — Auth & Settings
info.description:
The Orebit identity surface: registration, login, sessions, two-factor, and the security settings a signed-in user controls — including the Payment PIN.

─── How to use it ───

1. Set `baseUrl` (defaults to http://localhost:3000).
2. Sign in with `2. Login — POST /auth/login — password`. Its test script stores `accessToken` and `csrfToken` for you; every authenticated request inherits the bearer token from the collection.
3. Refresh and device cookies are set by the server and replayed by Postman automatically — do not send them by hand.

─── Multi-action routes ───

Several endpoints take a discriminated union (`step`, `mode`, `action`, `method`). Those appear once per action, named `METHOD /path — action`, because one request with ten mutually exclusive bodies squashed together would be worse than nothing.

Labels are owned by `docs/postman/generate.ts`; bodies are curated here. `tests/auth/openapi.drift.spec.ts` fails if a live route has no request.

─── Security cooldown after an email change ───

For 24 hours after the account's email address changes, these are frozen and answer `security_change_cooldown` (403) with a `Retry-After` header and `extra.availableAt`:

- folder 4 — `set` and `change` password
- folder 8 — `totp-add`, `totp-confirm`, `passkey-add-challenge`, `passkey-add-verify`, `recovery-regenerate`
- folder 10 — both factor surfaces, enable and disable
- folder 11 — the Payment PIN: enable, verify, update, disable

It stops an attacker who reaches an email change from taking the password, enrolling their own factor (collecting the account's first recovery codes on the way) and setting a PIN in the same minute. It is account state in one Postgres column, so logging out, signing in again or switching device does not clear it, and the check lives on the service method — switching from `/settings/security/*` to `/auth/2fa` reaches the same guard.

Folder 12 is deliberately exempt: email RECOVERY must work while the account is frozen, because that is the mechanism for undoing a change the owner did not make. The cooldown is 24 hours and is independent of the 30-day retained-address window — the two answer different questions.

item.name: 11. Payment PIN — /settings/security/payment-pin

request.description: Everything a client needs to render the screen: whether a PIN is set, whether one may be created, which verification methods are open, and how many changes remain in the current window. The frontend never has to work out whether the account has an authenticator or a passkey — that is decided here.

One request, no challenge: enabling is authorised by the emailed code plus the EXISTENCE of a passkey or authenticator, which the backend checks itself.

Refused with `mfa_method_unavailable` when neither factor is enrolled — the PIN must not become the account's only self-service credential.

The PIN must be exactly 6 digits and not trivially guessable: `000000`, `123456`, `121212` and the like are refused with `payment_pin_weak`.

Refused with `security_change_cooldown` (403) while the account is inside the security cooldown — the 24 hours after its email address changes. The response carries a `Retry-After` header and `extra.availableAt`, so the client renders a deadline rather than a dead end. See the collection description.

Set `operation` to `update` or `disable` — the challenge is bound to it and will not work for the other.

Send exactly the proof your declared method names. A request carrying `currentPin` AND `totpCode` is refused as ambiguous rather than resolved in the server's favour.

Needs a challenge verified for `update`. No `userId`, no `method`, no `currentPin` — the server already knows all three from the verification.

Capped at 3 changes per 24 hours per ACCOUNT, shared across all three verification methods and not reset by signing in again. `remaining` on the GET tells you what is left.

The new PIN must differ from the current one (`payment_pin_reused`).

Removes the PIN outright — the stored hash is deleted, not retired. Your other sessions are NOT signed out: a Payment PIN never established a session, so there is nothing for a sweep to invalidate. The account owner is emailed.

item.name: 12. Email — /settings/security/email
item.description:
Changing the account's email address, and undoing a change that was not the owner's doing.

─── Change ───
  GET  /settings/security/email                    → securityMethods, remaining
  POST /settings/security/email  {action:'start'}  → challengeId + requiredTargets
  (read the code in EACH mailbox it names)
  POST /settings/security/email/verify             → address moved

The tier and the address are fixed at `start` and read from the server's record at completion, so neither can be swapped afterwards. Every session is revoked on success — including this one, so sign in again before using the rest of the collection.

─── Recovery ───

The released address receives a “did you do this?” message carrying a single-use token. These two requests need NO SESSION: a completed change revokes them all, and the released address cannot sign in, so the person who needs this is exactly the one who cannot authenticate.
  POST /settings/security/email  {action:'recover-start'}  → code to the old address
  POST /settings/security/email/verify                     → account restored or redirected

Set `emailRecoveryToken` from the link in that email first. Recovery does not spend a change-budget slot.

request.description: Everything the screen needs: the address (masked), which security tier a change would require, how many changes remain, and whether a previous address is still on hold.

Set `emailMethod` to one of `change.securityMethods` from the GET. Add "skipRetainedEmail": true only when a previous mailbox is unreachable — it needs an authenticator, passkey or KYC, and it expires that retention.
One mailbox at a time — `current`, `new` or `retained`. Resending everything would invalidate the codes you have already found.

Add the proof your tier needs: `totpCode`, `passkey`, `kyc`, or `password`. The `none` tier takes none. Add `retainedEmailCode` only when `requiredTargets` included `retained`.

Sending two proofs is refused before any comparison runs, and `method` must match the one the change was started with.

On success this STARTS the security cooldown: `users.email_changed_at` is set in the same transaction that moves the address, and for the next 24 hours the account cannot change its 2FA, recovery codes, Payment PIN or password. Folders 4, 8, 10 and 11 will answer `security_change_cooldown`.

NO SESSION REQUIRED. intent "restore" puts the account back on the released address. For intent "replace" add "newEmail" and a code goes to both mailboxes. "reportedCompromise" marks it as “this wasn’t me” — same mutation, different notification.

NOT blocked by the security cooldown, and that exemption is the point. A change revokes every session and the released address cannot sign in, so the person who needs recovery is precisely the one who cannot authenticate — and a live retention plus a fresh `email_changed_at` are always present here. Freezing this would close the flow for every legitimate recovery there will ever be.

A `restore` CLEARS the cooldown (the change has been undone, and the owner needs their password and factors back). A `replace` RESTARTS it — the account has moved somewhere new, which is an email change by every meaning the policy has.

NO SESSION REQUIRED, and no security factor: the token proves the mailbox. Add `newEmailCode` for a replace; it is refused on a restore.

On success every session is revoked and the address that had taken over is released outright, with no reservation of its own.

Freezing this would close the flow for every legitimate recovery there will ever be.
